title-group.article-title: Exploring LEPR-Linked Metabolic Diversity through Gut Microbiome-Metabolome Network Analysis in Non-Obese Adults

abstract.p: Genetic variation in the leptin receptor (LEPR) gene has been implicated in metabolic regulation, while the gut microbiome and circulating metabolites are increasingly recognized as mediators of host metabolic phenotype. However, the systems-level interactions among LEPR genotypes, gut microbial composition, and serum metabolomic profiles remain poorly understood, particularly in healthy individuals. We conducted a cross-sectional study involving 37 healthy Korean adults. Three LEPR single nucleotide polymorphisms (rs1137101, rs1173100, rs790419) were genotyped. Untargeted metabolomics of fasting serum was performed using gas chromatography–time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and gut microbiome composition was profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Statistical analysis included principal component analysis, Mann–Whitney U tests, and Spearman correlations. Network analysis integrating microbiome, metabolomic, and clinical phenotype data was conducted using Cytoscape. A total of 54 serum metabolites were identified. LEPR genotypes, particularly rs1137101 and rs1173100, were associated with differences in metabolites such as pimelic acid, malonic acid, and 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid. Firmicutes negatively correlated with saturated fatty acids and organic acids, whereas Actinobacteria positively correlated with cholesterol and amino acids. Network analysis revealed indole-3-acetate and cholesterol as central nodes linking microbial taxa with body mass index and leptin levels. However, no direct molecular pathways connecting leptin or its receptor were identified. LEPR genetic variation is associated with distinct serum metabolomic patterns and microbiome–host networks in healthy adults. Although no direct leptin signaling links were found, network-level associations suggest indirect genetic influences on metabolic states through microbiome–metabolome interactions. These findings advance understanding of personalized metabolic regulation and gene–microbiome interplay.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Obesity is a complex metabolic disorder influenced by genetic, environmental, and microbial factors (Vallianou et al., 2019). Among the genetic contributors, polymorphisms in the leptin receptor gene (LEPR) have been implicated in regulating energy balance, appetite, and adiposity (Friedman, 2019). The rs1137101 (Q223R) variant of the LEPR gene, in particular, has been associated with altered leptin signaling and obesity-related phenotypes in multiple populations (Supti et al., 2024; Yuliawati et al., 2024). In parallel, increasing evidence supports the role of the gut microbiome in host metabolism and systemic energy regulation (Delzenne et al., 2019), with compositional differences observed between lean and obese individuals. However, while both LEPR polymorphisms and gut microbial composition have independently been linked to obesity risk (Górczyńska-Kosiorz et al., 2024), little is known about their functional interplay in healthy individuals. Our previous study (Cha et al., 2023) demonstrated a significant association between the LEPR rs1137101 genotype and the relative abundance of Candidatus Saccharibacteria in the gut microbiome of healthy, non-obese Korean adults. Building upon this finding, we hypothesized the LEPR polymorphisms may also influence host metabolic phenotypes as reflected by serum metabolomic profiles, independent of body weight. To test this, we conducted an untargeted metabolomics analysis of serum samples collected from the same clinical cohort, aiming to elucidate the functional consequences of LEPR genetic variation on systemic metabolic states and their potential linkage to the gut microbial ecosystem.

Untargeted metabolomics offers a comprehensive snapshot of the host’s metabolic state, reflecting both endogenous processes and interactions with the gut microbiota (Kumar et al., 2020). In particular, gut microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids, biogenic amines, and amino acid derivatives are increasingly recognized as key mediators of host-microbe communication, with systemic effects on insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, and inflammatory pathways (Rooks and Garrett, 2016). Moreover, recent studies have proposed that genetic variation in host metabolic regulators, such as LEPR, may shape the gut microbiome and its metabolic output via bidirectional signaling along the gut-liver axis (De Cól et al., 2024). This axis plays a central role in nutrient sensing and energy homeostasis and is increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases (Tilg et al., 2022). Despite these insights, few studies have directly examined how LEPR genetic polymorphisms modulate the circulating metabolome in relation to gut microbial composition, particularly in healthy individuals without confounding factors such as obesity or comorbid disease. By integrating genotype, microbiome, and metabolomic data from a well-characterized healthy Korean cohort, this study aims to uncover novel functional relationships that may serve as early biomarkers or therapeutic targets in precision metabolic health management.

In this study, we sought to investigate whether LEPR single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are associated with distinct patterns in the serum metabolome of healthy Korean adults, and whether these metabolic signatures correlate with previously observed alterations in gut microbial composition. By employing gas chromatography time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC-TOF-MS) for untargeted metabolomic profiling, we identified key metabolites whose circulating levels differ according to LEPR genotype. These findings were integrated with microbial taxonomic data and clinical variables to explore potential genotype-microbiome-metabolome interactions.

sec.title: Study design and Ethical approval
sec.p: This study was a prospective, single-center, observational study conducted at the Clinical Trials Center of Chungnam National University Hospital (Daejeon, Korea). The study design, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and clinical procedures were identical to those described in our previously published work investigating the association between LEPR genotypes and gut microbiome composition in healthy Korean adults (Cha et al., 2023). Briefly, healthy volunteers aged 19-50 years with a body mass index between 18.0 and 25.0 kg/m2 were enrolled after providing written informed consent. Participants who had taken antibiotics within one month prior to enrollment were excluded.

The study protocol and all related procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Chungnam National University Hospital (IRB No. CNUH 2022-07-043) and were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Korean Good Clinical Practice (KGCP) guidelines.

sec.title: Study participants and clinical data collection
sec.p: From the original cohort of 65 healthy volunteers described in our previous study (Cha et al., 2023), a total of 37 participants were finally included in this study. Twenty-eight participants were excluded because their serum samples did not meet the stringent quality control criteria for GC-TOF-MS analysis (e.g., insufficient signal-to-noise ratio or retention time shifts). This selection process ensured that only high-quality metabolomic data were used for the subsequent multi-omics integration.

All participants underwent standardized clinical evaluations, including measurement of anthropometric indices (age, sex, height, weight, body mass index), vital signs, and laboratory tests at screening. Blood samples were collected following an overnight fast, processed within 30 min, and stored at –70°C until further analysis. Only serum samples that met predefined quality control criteria for metabolomic analysis – such as signal-to-noise ratio, retention time stability, and total ion count consistency – were included in this study.

sec.title: LEPR genotyping
sec.p: Genotyping of three leptin receptor SNPs – rs1173100 (K109R), rs1137101 (Q223R), and rs790419 (S343S) – was conducted as previously described (Cha et al., 2023). Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood samples using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen GmbH, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The rs1173100 and rs1137101 SNPs were genotyped using the TaqMan SNP Genotyping Assay (Applied Biosystems, MA, USA) with pre-designed primer/probe sets (C_7586955_10 and C_8722581_10, respectively). PCR amplification was carried out using the StepOnePlusTM Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) with the following thermal cycling conditions: 95°C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of 92°C for 15 s and 60°C for 90 s.

For rs790419, genotyping was performed by PCR amplification and direct sequencing using the following primers: forward 5’-TCCAAACAAGACAATAGCGGC-3′ and reverse 5′-CCTCGAGGTTTGGTTTCATTCA-3′. The amplified 674 bp products were sequenced with the same primers.

sec.title: GC-TOF-MS analysis
sec.p: A GC-MS based metabolome was profiled from serum samples. A fasting serum was thawed on ice and 100 μL of serum sample and pooled serum used as a quality control sample was mixed with 1 mL of first extraction solution (3:3:2, acetonitrile:isopropanol:H2O). Then, a 400 μL of extracts after centrifugation (5 min at 18,341×g and 4°C) and dried under streams of nitrogen gas. Subsequently, 0.4 mL of second extraction solution (1:1, acetonitrile:H2O) was added to the dried residue and the extract was dried again after the centrifugation. For chemical derivatization, methoxyamine (20 mg/mL in pyridine) was treated to the sample at 30°C for 90 min and subsequently trimethylsilylated with a mixture of fatty acid methyl ester (used for the retention time index) in N-methyl-N-(trimethylsilyl)-trifluoroacetamide at 70°C for 45 min, and injection into the GC-TOF-MS system (Agilent 7890B Gas Chromatography coupled to Leco Pegasus HT TOF-MS) as demonstrated previously (Lee et al., 2021). The raw data was processed using ChromaTOF software version 4.72 and metabolites were annotated using publicly available MS spectrum libraries and in-house MS library. Finally, a total of 54 metabolites were identified from serum cohort. Features that show high variability (relative standard deviation over 30% regarding in the quality control samples) were waived and the peak intensities were further normalized using MetaboAnalyst 5.0 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca).

sec.title: Gut microbiome analysis
sec.p: Stool samples were collected using a commercial stool collection kit containing nucleic acid stabilizers (NBgene-GUT kit; Noble Biosciences, Seoul, Korea), immediately frozen below –70°C, and analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. The detailed procedures for DNA extraction, PCR amplification, sequencing, and taxonomic classification were identified to those described in our previous publication (Cha et al., 2023).

Briefly, microbial DNA was extracted using the Chemagic DNA Stool Kit (PerkinElmer, MA, USA), including a bead-beating pretreatment. The V4 hypervariable region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the NEXTflex 16S V4 Amplicon-Seq Kit (BioO Scientific, Austin, TX, USA), and sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform (500 cycles, v2 kit). A minimum of 20,000 reads per sample were obtained.

Sequencing data were processed using the QIIME2 pipeline. Quality filtering and denoising were performed with DADA2, and taxonomic classification was conducted using naïve Bayes classifiers trained on the NCBI RefSeq database via the q2-feature-classifier plugin. Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) with low prevalence or read count were excluded. Microbial composition was analyzed at the phylum level, and only taxa with relative abundance above 0.1% were included in downstream analyses.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed to evaluate differences in serum metabolite levels according to LEPR genotypes and to assess associations between metabolomic features, gut microbial taxa, and clinical variables.

Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted to assess overall patterns in metabolomic data and to evaluate technical variability using pooled quality control samples. Univariate analysis comparing metabolite intensities between LEPR genotype groups (e.g., rs1137101 G/G vs. G/A) was performed using the Mann-Whitney U test, and the results were visualized using volcano plots combining fold change and p-value criteria. A fold change threshold of ±1.2 and a p-value cutoff of 0.05 were applied for significance.

Spearman rank correlation analysis was used to assess the associations between serum metabolites and relative abundances of gut microbiota at the phylum level, as well as between serum metabolites and clinical parameters (e.g., leptin concentration, lipid profiles). All metabolite intensity data were log-transformed and normalized prior to statistical testing to reduce variance and skewness.

Statistical analyses and data visualization were performed using GraphPad Prism (v9.5.1, GraphPad Software, CA, USA) and MetaboAnalyst 5.0. A two-tailed p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Network pharmacology analysis
sec.p: To investigate the systems-level relationships between gut microbiota, circulating plasma metabolites, and clinical traits including leptin-related phenotypes, a network pharmacology analysis was conducted using Cytoscape (v3.10.3, National Human Genome Research Institute, USA). An edge list was constructed based on the results of Spearman correlation analyses between gut microbial phyla, serum metabolites, and clinical parameters (e.g., leptin concentration, BMI, HDL, LDL, and triglycerides). Only associations with an absolute correlation coefficient greater than 0.3 were retained to ensure biological relevance and reduce network complexity.

The resulting edge list was imported into Cytoscape and visualized as a tripartite network connecting microbial phyla, metabolites, and host phenotypes. Node attributes were manually assigned according to biological category (i.e., Microbiome, Metabolite, Clinical parameter). Network edges were mapped according to correlation direction and strength, with edge thickness scaled to correlation magnitude.

For metabolic pathway enrichment and functional contextualization, the MetScape 3.1.3 plugin was employed. Identified serum metabolites were queried using compound names and cross-referenced with standard KEGG identifiers when available. MetScape was used to generate compound-reaction-gene-pathway subnetworks for key metabolites of interest (e.g., indole-3-acetate and cholesterol), which were differentially associated with both microbial taxa and leptin-related phenotypes.

sec.title: Participants’ demographics
sec.p: A total of 37 healthy Korean adults (35 females and 2 males) were included in the final analysis. The mean age of participants was 36.1 ± 6.5 years, and the average body mass index (BMI) was 21.9 ± 1.5 kg/m², consistent with the inclusion criteria for non-obese individuals. The mean serum leptin concentration was 12,270.3 ± 10,114.3 pg/mL. Lipid profile parameters were within normal ranges: HDL cholesterol was 71.5 ± 12.3 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol was 104.8 ± 17.2 mg/dL, and triglycerides were 82.1 ± 33.3 mg/dL.

Genotype frequencies for the LEPR SNPs were as follows: for rs1173100 (K109R), 6 participants were homozygous A/A, 21 heterozygous G/A, and 10 homozygous G/G; for rs1137101 (Q223R), 28 participants were homozygous G/G and 9 heterozygous G/A; for rs790419 (Ser343Ser), 34 participants were homozygous T/T and 3 heterozygous T/C. No homozygous variant for the C allele was observed at rs790419.

sec.title: Serum metabolites identification
sec.p: Untargeted metabolomic profiling of serum samples using GC-TOF-MS resulted in the identification of 54 unique metabolites across all quality control-qualified participants (N=37). Metabolites were annotated based on retention index and spectral matching with an in-house reference library, ensuring high confidence in compound identification.

The identified metabolites encompassed a diverse range of biochemical classes, including: fatty acids (e.g., palmitic acid, oleic acid), amino acids (e.g., valine, isoleucine), gut microbiota-derived metabolites (e.g., 3-hydroxybutyric acid, indole derivatives), biogenic amines and other organic acids (Table 1).

The distribution of these metabolites was consistent with known serum biochemical profiles in healthy individuals (Agueusop et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024). All samples exhibited a high degree of spectral reproducibility, and no technical outliers were identified during PCA-based quality control assessment.

A subset of metabolites demonstrated notable inter-individual variability, suggesting potential genotype- or microbiota-dependent metabolic phenotypes. These metabolites were further investigated in downstream correlation and genotype-based analysis.

sec.title: Spearman correlation of Phylum vs. metabolites and Clinical laboratory test vs. metabolites
sec.p: To assess the overall structure and technical reproducibility of the serum metabolomic dataset, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on all identified metabolites across study participants and quality control samples. The PCA score plot revealed that test samples were evenly distributed around the centroid formed by pooled quality control samples, indicating high analytical stability throughout the acquisition process (Fig. 1). No outlier samples were detected based on PCA distribution, further supporting the robustness of the metabolite quantification across biological replicates.

To explore potential functional linkages between gut microbial composition and host metabolic states, spearman correlation analyses were conducted between the relative abundances of major gut microbial phyla and the levels of individual serum metabolites. Among the detected phyla, several exhibited significant associations with specific metabolite features (Fig. 2).

Firmicutes showed the most widespread negative correlations, with significant inverse associations (ρ<–0.25) observed for multiple metabolites including 2,3-dihydroxybutyric acid (ρ=–0.31), cholesterol (ρ=–0.30), alanine (ρ=–0.34), citric acid (ρ=–0.29), and several saturated fatty acids such as decanoic acid and myristic acid. In contrast, 3-indoleacetic acid was positively associated with Firmicutes (ρ=0.34), suggesting involvement in microbial tryptophan metabolism. Actinobacteria exhibited primarily positive correlations with serum metabolites. Notably, it was strongly associated (ρ>0.30) with cholesterol (ρ=0.35), alanine (ρ=0.34), and threonine (ρ=0.39). These patterns suggest that Actinobacteria may contribute to host amino acid and lipid metabolism. Lentisphaerae showed a mixed pattern but demonstrated positive associations with indole derivatives (3-indoleacetic acid, ρ=0.25), boric acid (ρ=0.29), and energy-related intermediates such as a-ketoglutarate and hypoxanthine. Synergistetes showed moderate positive correlations with 3-indoleacetic acid (ρ=0.31), succinate (ρ=0.17), and a-ketoglutarate (ρ=0.16), consistent with its potential role in amino acid fermentation and host–microbe co-metabolism. Proteobacteria and Spirochaetes exhibited heterogeneous associations. While both phyla showed modest correlations with organic acids and microbial metabolites, no strong or coherent trend across metabolic classes was observed. In contrast, Bacteroidetes showed largely weak or inverse associations with core energy-related metabolites. However, it exhibited mild positive correlations with myristic acid and palmitic acid, indicating a potential role in lipid metabolism.

Spearman correlation analysis revealed that several serum metabolites exhibited notable associations with clinical laboratory parameters, including BMI, leptin, HDL, LDL, and triglyceride (TG) levels.

Leptin levels were negatively correlated with several short-chain organic acids and lipid metabolites, including 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid (ρ=–0.43), glyceric acid (ρ=–0.37), lactoyl-lactic acid (ρ=–0.41), and p-cresol sulfate (ρ=–0.34). These findings suggest a possible link between leptin signaling and microbial or host-derived oxidative metabolites. BMI was positively associated with leucine (ρ=0.31), malic acid (ρ=0.37), and valine (ρ=0.29), while negatively correlated with glyceric acid (ρ=–0.34) and malonate (ρ=–0.26). This pattern reflects potential metabolic adaptations associated with adiposity, including shifts in amino acid and organic acid metabolism. HDL cholesterol exhibited strong inverse correlations with several amino acids and biogenic amines such as glycine (ρ=–0.44), leucine (ρ=–0.39), valine (ρ=–0.41), and tyrosine (ρ=–0.30). In contrast, glyceric acid (ρ=0.46) and glycerol (ρ=0.35) were positively associated with HDL, suggesting that higher HDL levels may reflect enhanced oxidative or glycerol-based energy metabolism. TG levels were negatively correlated with p-cresol sulfate (ρ=–0.46), glyceric acid (ρ=–0.43), and uric acid (ρ=–0.41), while positively associated with leucine (ρ=0.36), 3-indoleacetic acid (ρ=0.33), and valine (ρ=0.25). These patterns point to a possible linkage between circulating amino acids, microbial-derived metabolites, and lipid metabolism. LDL cholesterol showed fewer consistent associations, though mild positive correlations were noted with alanine, malic acid, and valine, suggesting a more limited role of LDL in shaping the metabolomic landscape in this healthy cohort.

sec.title: Mann-Whitney U test of LEPR SNP vs. metabolites
sec.p: Genotype distribution among the study participants is summarized in Table 2. The rs1137101 locus exhibited the most common variation, with 28 participants carrying the GG genotype and 9 carrying GA. These results suggest that LEPR rs1137101 may be associated with variations in specific circulating metabolites in healthy adults, independent of obesity status.

Univariate analysis using the Mann-Whitney U test revealed significant differences in the circulating levels of specific serum metabolites according to LEPR genotype. In particular, comparison between rs1173100 genotypes, four metabolic features were upregulated in GA allele group compared to AA alleles and seven metabolites were elevated in GG alleles, compared to AA alleles (Fig. 3A, 3B). Interestingly, pimelic acid and 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid were elevated in both GA and GG allele compared to AA allele. For rs1137101 genotypes (GA vs. GG) identified malonic acid, nonanoic acid, pimelic acid and 2-aminobutyric acid with differential abundance as visualized in volcano plots (Fig. 3C). Statistical analysis for rs790419 variants was limited due to the low frequency of the minor allele (TC=3) compared to the major allele (TT=34).

sec.title: Network pharmacology analysis of microbiome-metabolome-host interactions
sec.p: To elucidate the interconnections between the gut microbiome, circulating metabolites, and host metabolic phenotypes, a correlation-based network was constructed. The final network consisted of 45 nodes and 57 edges, comprising three categories of elements: microbial phyla, serum metabolites, and clinical traits including BMI, leptin, HDL, LDL, and triglyceride (Fig. 4).

Nodes were classified by biological category and displayed distinct patterns of connectivity. Several metabolites demonstrated high centrality, forming hubs that linked multiple microbial taxa with host metabolic parameters. In particular, indole-3-acetate (IAA) and cholesterol exhibited strong associations with multiple microbial phyla – such as Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Synergistetes, and Tenericutes.

The prominence of IAA and cholesterol in connecting microbiota with leptin-related host traits prompted further metabolic contextualization. MetScape-based pathway analysis (Fig. 5) showed that IAA was embedded in tryptophan metabolism and associated with enzymes linked to aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) activation, while cholesterol was positioned within steroid biosynthesis and bile acid metabolism networks. Although AhR itself is not explicitly shown in the network, IAA is a well-characterized microbial tryptophan catabolite known to function as an endogenous ligand of AhR (Hubbard et al., 2015; Vrzalová et al., 2022; Vyhlídalová et al., 2020). In Fig. 5(b), IAA is positioned within the tryptophan metabolism pathway and is connected to enzymatic reactions, including those catalyzed by aldehyde dehydrogenase, which contribute to its biosynthesis (Shatova and Shestopalov, 2023). These connections highlight the potential role of IAA in modulating AhR-mediated signaling pathways.

The network also revealed a distinct cluster of dicarboxylic acids and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) derivatives, including 2,4-dihydroxybutanoic acid, oxalic acid, and 2-hydroxypropanoic acid dimer, that were directly linked to leptin and BMI in the correlation-based network (Fig. 4). These metabolites formed a coherent subnetwork within MetScape-based pathway analysis (Fig. 5), mapping onto nodes associated with glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, and butanoate metabolism.

Although no hormone receptor-related genes were identified in the immediate vicinity of this subnetwork, the dicarboxylic acid-related metabolites—including 2,4-dihydroxybutanoic acid and oxalate—were enriched within metabolic pathways such as glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism and butanoate metabolism, based on MetScape network integration (Fig. 5). These compounds showed direct correlations with BMI and leptin levels in the correlation-based network (Fig. 4), suggesting their relevance to metabolic traits associated with obesity. Dicarboxylic acids are intermediates in glyoxylate and butanoate metabolism, respectively, and have been previously studied in the context of energy metabolism and redox balance (Fanjul et al., 2015; Sahin and Beyazci̇cek, 2023; Zahid et al., 2023). However, no direct association with leptin or leptin receptor signaling was found in our analysis.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study demonstrates that specific LEPR polymorphisms – particularly rs1137101 and rs1173100 – are associated with significant alterations in serum metabolite profiles in healthy, non-obese adults. These findings extend previous observations that primarily focused on obese populations (Almeida et al., 2018; Maculewicz et al., 2022, Raskiliene et al., 2021), highlighting that LEPR genotypes may influence systemic metabolism even in the absence of overt metabolic disease.

Among the metabolites showing genotype-dependent variation, pimelic acid, malonic acid, and 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid are of particular interest. Pimelic acid is a seven-carbon dicarboxylic acid involved in fatty acid degradation and biotin synthesis (Liu et al., 2020), and its elevated levels may reflect altered mitochondrial β-oxidation or peroxisomal activity (Zhao et al., 2022). Malonic acid, a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, has also been implicated in modulating oxidative metabolism and redox status (Rosa et al., 2021). 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid is a non-canonical intermediate in fatty acid metabolism (Curovic et al., 2024) and is associated with shifts in mitochondrial substrate utilization under conditions of metabolic stress (Amer et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2022). The observation that these metabolites differ significantly according to LEPR genotype supports the notion that LEPR variants may contribute to individual differences in mitochondrial efficiency, fatty acid oxidation, and intermediary metabolism. Although our data does not establish a direct mechanistic link between LEPR genotype and leptin signaling, prior studies have shown that the rs1137101 G allele is associated with reduced leptin binding affinity and altered energy homeostasis (Daghestani et al., 2019; Supti et al., 2024). These metabolic alterations may thus represent downstream adaptive responses to genetically encoded differences in leptin receptor function, even in metabolically healthy individuals

To further explore the functional context of these genotype-associated metabolic alterations, our network pharmacology analysis was conducted. This analysis revealed that several of these same metabolite classes, including multiple dicarboxylic acids, alongside other key metabolites like IAA and cholesterol, occupy central positions in the microbiome-metabolome-phenotype network. These central metabolites act as integrative nodes connecting gut microbial taxa with host clinical parameters such as BMI and serum leptin concentrations, suggesting their potential role as mediators of gut-host metabolic communication.

Among these, IAA-a microbial tryptophan catabolite-exhibited prominent centrality, linking multiple phyla (e.g., Firmicutes, Synergistetes) to host metabolic traits. Enrichment analysis positioned IAA within the tryptophan metabolism pathway, where it is known to engage the AhR, a ligand-activated transcription factor involved in immune regulation and intestinal homeostasis (Han et al., 2021). These findings align with prior reports demonstrating the capacity of IAA to modulate gut-liver axis function through AhR-dependent pathways, thereby suggesting an immunometabolic signaling axis influenced by the microbiome (Min et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Similarly, cholesterol was identified as a hub metabolite, with connections to both microbial phyla and host lipid parameters. Its presence within the steroid biosynthesis and bile acid metabolism pathways highlights its potential role in mediating microbiota-host interactions, possibly through modulation of enterohepatic circulation. However, its connection to leptin signaling appears to be indirect and likely reflects broader shifts in host lipidomic status rather than LEPR-specific regulation. Nevertheless, considering that LEPR signaling in the central nervous system regulates energy homeostasis (Maffei and Giordano, 2022), these systemic effects could be mediated through the gut-brain-liver axis. Specifically, LEPR genetic variations might modulate vagal nerve signaling or alter bile acid secretion, thereby reshaping the gut microenvironment and influencing microbial metabolic output.

Notably, a group of dicarboxylic acids and SCFA derivatives – including 2,4-dihydroxybutanoic acid, oxalic acid, and 2-hydroxypropanoic acid dimer – also emerged as central components of the network. These metabolites demonstrated significant correlations with BMI and serum leptin concentrations, suggesting a potential role in energy homeostasis. Dicarboxylic acids such as oxalate and 2,4-hydroxybutanoate are recognized intermediates of alternative fatty acid oxidation and are reflective of hepatic mitochondrial substrate preference under metabolic stress (Zhang et al., 2021) Previous studies have linked elevations in these metabolites to impaired β-oxidation, oxidative stress, and compensatory upregulation of the glyoxylate shunt and dicarboxylate pathways, particularly in insulin-resistant or nutrient-overloaded states (Castagneto-Gissey et al., 2024; Krishnamurthy and Liotta, 2023; Zhang et al., 2018).

The enrichment of glyoxylate and butanoate metabolism pathways in our MetScape-based functional analysis further supports the notion of a systemic metabolic adaptation. Butanoate metabolism, driven by microbiota-derived SCFA production, is essential for maintaining gut barrier integrity (Bach Knudsen et al., 2018) and modulating lipid metabolism (Yu et al., 2019), while intermediates from pyruvate metabolism (e.g., lactoyl-lactate, glyceric acid) suggest shifts in cellular redox state and mitochondrial energetics (Louis and Flint, 2017). Importantly, while these metabolites were statistically associated with leptin levels in our network, they are not known to participate in canonical leptin or LEPR signaling pathways. Rather, their centrality may reflect broader metabolic adaptations to genetically or microbially mediated perturbations in host energy metabolism.

A central finding of this integrated analysis is that the metabolites identified as genotype-dependent (e.g., pimelic acid, 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid, malonic acid, as shown in Fig. 3) are the same metabolites and metabolic classes (dicarboxylic acids, SCFA derivatives) that emerged as central hubs in the network analysis (Fig. 4). Although LEPR genotypes were not explicit nodes in the network model, this convergence provided a direct genotype-centered interpretation: the network hubs reflect the functional integration of those metabolites most strongly influenced by LEPR variation. This suggests that LEPR variation shapes systemic metabolism not by direct pairwise associations, but through subtle modulation of these key metabolite classes that constitute integrative nodes in the microbiome-metabolome-host network.

Prior work indicates that leptin signaling influences fatty acid oxidation and acylcarnitine turnover, while microbial SCFAs and indole metabolites can modulate leptin secretion and signaling through G-protein–coupled and AhR pathways (Suzuki et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2024). These converging lines of evidence suggest that LEPR variation may shape systemic metabolism not by direct pairwise associations, but through subtle modulation of metabolite classes that constitute integrative nodes in the microbiome–metabolome–host network.

The findings of this study provide novel insights into how host genetic variation can influence metabolic phenotype in healthy, non-obese individuals through indirect interactions with the gut microbiome and circulating metabolites. By integrating genotypic, microbiomics, and metabolomic data, we identified systems-level associations that may precede overt metabolic dysregulation, suggesting that even in the absence of clinical obesity, genetic determinants of leptin signaling can shape host energy metabolism via microbial and metabolic intermediates.

This multi-omics framework supports a paradigm in which genetic predispositions do not operate in isolation but interact with microbial ecosystems to modulate host metabolic homeostasis. The identification of central metabolites such as IAA, cholesterol, and dicarboxylic acids highlights their potential as sentinel intermediates reflective of these gene-microbiome-metabolite networks. Importantly, the study underscores the value of investigating metabolic diversity in healthy populations. By capturing LEPR genotype-dependent metabolic shifts prior to the onset of obesity, our findings turn the limitation of a small cohort into a strength, providing a reference dataset for future large-scale longitudinal cohorts focused on sub-clinical metabolic risk. These early deviations in molecular profiles could serve as ‘sentinel biomarkers’ to identify healthy individuals at higher genetic risk for metabolic dysregulation. This, in turn, may inform targeted preventive strategies or early interventions - such as personalized nutrition or microbiome modulation – aimed at optimizing metabolic resilience long before clinical disease manifests. For instance, individuals carrying the LEPR rs1137101 GG genotype, who exhibit distinct metabolite profiles, might benefit from personalized dietary interventions – such as tryptophan-rich diets to modulate IAA levels – based on the microbiome-metabolome interactions identified in our network analysis (Fig. 6).

However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional nature of the study precludes causal inference regarding the directionality of observed associations among genotype, microbiome composition, and metabolite levels. Longitudinal studies or interventional designs will be needed to validate the temporal dynamics of these interactions. Second, the modest sample size (N=37) limits statistical power for stratified analyses by genotype, sex, or other covariates. As such, our findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Third, the gut microbiome analysis was restricted to the phylum level. While finer taxonomic resolution could provide more detailed insights, the high dimensionality of such data would require a significantly larger sample size to ensure statistical robustness. Given the modest sample size (N=37) and the resolution limits of 16S rRNA V4 amplicon sequencing, we focused on macro-level microbial shifts to minimize false discovery rates and avoid overinterpretation. Lastly, the functional implications of the identified metabolic pathways – particularly in relation to leptin receptor signaling – remain speculative and would benefit from experimental validation in cellular or animal models.

Despite these limitations, this study provides a foundational step toward understanding how LEPR-linked genetic variation may contribute to inter-individual differences in metabolic phenotype through microbiome-modulated pathways. This work serves as an exploratory pilot study demonstrating that LEPR genetic variations are linked to systemic metabolic profiles in healthy adults. Future studies with larger cohorts and deeper microbial sequencing are warranted to validate these findings and further elucidate the molecular architecture underlying personalized metabolic regulation at a finer resolution.

Heatmap of Spearman correlations between (A) gut microbial phyla vs. serum metabolites and (B) clinical laboratory tests vs. serum metabolites in healthy Korean adults. *p-value <0.05; **p-value <0.01.

Volcano plots of serum metabolites according to LEPR genotype. Significant differences in circulating serum metabolite levels were identified using the Mann-Whitney U test. The x-axis represents the log2 fold change (FC), and the y-axis represents the -log10 p-value. Vertical lines indicate the significance threshold of FC +- 1.2, and the horizontal line indicates a p-value of 0.05. (A) Comparison of serum metabolite profiles between rs1173100 GA and AA genotypes (B) Comparison between rs1173100 GG and AA genotypes (C) Comparison between rs1137101 GA and GG genotypes.

Correlation-based network integrating gut microbial phyla, serum metabolites, and clinical parameters. A tripartite network was constructed using Spearman correlation coefficients (|ρ| >0.3) among gut microbiota (phylum level), serum metabolites, and clinical traits including BMI (body mass index), leptin, HDL (high-density lipoprotein), LDL (low-density lipoprotein), and triglyceride. Nodes are color-coded according to category: microbiome (green), metabolite (yellow), and clinical parameter (blue). Edge width reflects the magnitude of the correlation, and edge color indicates direction (red for positive, blue for negative).

Metabolite-centered metabolic pathway network generated by MetScape. (A) Overview of the whole compound-reaction-enzyme-gene network constructed from input metabolites identified in the correlation-based microbiome-metabolite-phenotype analysis. (B) Redrawn part of the subnetwork centered on cholesterol. (C) Redrawn part of the subnetwork centered on indole-3-acetate and its surroundings. Red hexagons represent input metabolites. Green rectangles indicate enzyme nodes, beige diamonds denote reactions, and blue circles represent associated genes. Arrows indicate directionality of biochemical reactions as defined in the KEGG pathway database. The network was generated using MetScape 3.1.3 in Cytoscape 3.10.3 and includes compounds with mapped KEGG IDs and their associated metabolic reactions and gene products.

Schematic summary of LEPR genotype-linked metabolic diversity and microbiome-metabolome interactions. Genetic variations in LEPR (rs1137101, rs1173100) are associated with distinct systemic metabolic profiles, characterized by alterations in dicarboxylic acids (pimelic acid, malonic acid) and 2,4-dihydroxybutyric acid. Network analysis highlights indole-3-acetate and cholesterol as central hubs bridging specific gut microbial taxa (e.g., Firmicutes, Actinobacteria) with host metabolic phenotypes. These interactions may be mediated via the gut-brain-liver axis and serve as ‘sentinel biomarkers’ for sub-clinical metabolic risk, offering a basis for precision nutrition strategies (e.g., tryptophan modulation) in healthy individuals.
